title: Sanada Yukimura Never Used That Name? 4 Letters｜Curio Archive
description:
Did Japan's legendary Sengoku warrior Sanada Yukimura—"Japan's Greatest Warrior"—ever actually call himself "Yukimura" while alive?
For anyone who knows the name from history, dramas, or games and wants to see what his own surviving letters really signed.

None of the lifetime documents examined so far use the name "Yukimura." In 1917, Tokyo Imperial University's Dai Nihon Shiryo printed a full-size foldout plate titled "Letter of Sanada Yukimura," yet the signature at the end reads "Sanada Saemon-no-suke Nobushige." From a note in Kudoyama asking for shochu ("Kohaku Nobushige") to three letters written inside Osaka Castle in 1615 before his death on the 7th day of the 5th month (June 3, 1615), every signature uses Nobushige or his court title Saemon-no-suke. Even Tokugawa-side reports—Hosokawa Tadaoki's dispatches and the Satsuma report recording the rumor "Sanada, Japan's greatest warrior"—call him only Sanada or Sanada Saemon, with "Yukimura" added later as an unbracketed side note in the Satsuma copy.

"Yukimura" is generally thought to appear earliest in the military chronicle Naniwa Senki (1672 preface; the base text examined is an undated expanded edition and rewritten in 1928). In Togen Iji, compiled after Tokugawa Mitsukuni died in early 1701, the retainers' small-print note already warned that calling him Yukimura was an error. When shogunate inspectors questioned the Sanada house in late 1809, retainers drafted a memo claiming he used Yukimura after entering Osaka—while admitting in the same memo that no book recorded such a name change. Then in 1911, a 25-sen Tachikawa Bunko pocket book made "Sanada Yukimura" a nationwide hero.

Who first coined "Yukimura" and why remains unknown in historical records. Letter texts follow Dai Nihon Shiryo; lunar dates follow the Japanese calendar; "I think" and "we think" mark this channel's commentary, with full sources below.

Information as of 2026-11-19

sv101.text: Japan's legendary warrior Sanada Yukimura—what if we've been calling him the wrong name?

sv102.text: Hailed as Japan's greatest warrior, the name Sanada Yukimura has echoed for centuries;

sv103.text: yet among lifetime records found so far, including four letters here, none say Yukimura.

sv104.text: In 1917, a Tokyo Imperial University collection printed one of those letters full-size as Yukimura's;

sv105.text: zoom in on the end, and the given name he signed is two completely different characters.

sv106.text: Yet a wartime dispatch right after his death prints tiny Yukimura beside his title;

sv107.text: Today let's see what real name his letters signed, and how Yukimura swept Japan.

sv201.text: From Ueda's Sanada clan in Shinano, a clan draft

sv202.text: lists him born in 1567, second son.

sv203.text: The Sanadas often used Yuki: grandfather Yukitaka, father Masayuki, son Yukimasa;

sv204.text: yet as an adult he didn't use Yuki,

sv205.text: taking real name Nobushige and title Saemon-no-suke—how did his letters sign?

sv206.text: To see letter one, look at his fall: in 1600, he and his father opposed victor Tokugawa Ieyasu and lost.

sv207.text: Spared execution, he was exiled to Mount Koya, then Kudoyama at its foot, for over a decade.

sv208.text: His first surviving letter comes from then: asking a man named Sakyo to send a jar of shochu.

sv209.text: Undated, it is signed with his Mount Koya title Kohaku plus his given name Nobushige;

sv210.text: so did he change his name to Yukimura later when returning to battle?

sv301.text: After over ten years in exile, Osaka Castle lord Toyotomi Hideyori invited him inside against the Tokugawa.

sv302.text: Letter two, 24th of the 1st month 1615, went from Osaka to sister Muramatsu.

sv303.text: It opens casually: someone was heading your way, so I'm sending a quick note, just like family mail;

sv304.text: It skips a given name, writing only his title Saemon-no-suke in kana—just a casual note?

sv305.text: Half a month later on the 10th of the 2nd month, letter three to Ishiai Juzo is a solemn farewell:

sv306.text: Having chosen to hold the castle, I am resolved to die; we will likely never meet again in this world.

sv307.text: Even this farewell signs only Sanada's first character plus Saemon-no-suke—did he stop signing any given name?

sv308.text: He did sign a name! On the 19th of the 3rd month, to brother-in-law Oyamada and son,

sv309.text: saying: Life is fleeting; count me out of this world.

sv310.text: That letter is the exact foldout plate from our opening, titled Letter of Sanada Yukimura;

sv311.text: at the end, he signed his title plus Nobushige, sealed with his personal monogram!

sv312.text: Once battle broke out, scholars verify six wooden merit plaques on the 6th of the 5th month signed Nobushige; next day he fell.

sv313.text: His own writings checked, let's flip angles: how did the rival Tokugawa camp call him?

sv401.text: Tokugawa camp letters tell us. Days after the battle, rival lord Hosokawa Tadaoki sent word home:

sv402.text: His first letter wrote only Sanada, and days later another praised Sanada Saemon-no-suke as unmatched in history.

sv403.text: Hosokawa wrote only surname and title; did that opening dispatch with tiny Yukimura call him that then?

sv404.text: Actually no! Written on the 11th of the 6th month, historians judge it came from a Tokugawa-side Shimazu samurai,

sv405.text: sent from Kyoto-Osaka to Satsuma, noting the famous praise: Japan's finest warrior,

sv406.text: yet the report's text writes only Sanada Saemon or Sanada.

sv407.text: First copied into Satsuma's Sappan Kyuki, then that collection—which stage added the gloss?

sv408.text: Tokyo University editors bracketed their notes while this gloss lacks brackets—likely added when Satsuma copied Sappan Kyuki.

sv409.text: When that copyist added it is unrecorded; among dated books, which is the earliest found writing Yukimura?

sv501.text: It is generally thought to be Naniwa Senki, a popular tale of the Osaka war with a 1672 preface.

sv502.text: Just fifty-seven years after the battle, it writes Saemon-no-suke Yukimura—you'd think case closed, right?

sv503.text: Yet our 1928 print uses an undated text,

sv504.text: with edits—so the original stays unsure.

sv505.text: Any firmly dated record? After Mito lord Tokugawa Mitsukuni died in early 1701, retainers compiled Togen Iji.

sv506.text: Compiled within the Tokugawa clan, it records Mitsukuni calling Sanada Nobuyori—not Yukimura either.

sv507.text: Stranger still, right beneath Nobuyori, the compiling retainers tucked a double-line note:

sv508.text: It says flatly: Calling him Yukimura is wrong. Note that the retainers wrote this, not Mitsukuni himself.

sv509.text: That note proves Yukimura was already widespread enough around 1701 that Mito retainers felt forced to correct it.

sv510.text: Yet Nobuyori still mismatches his letters, and later essays in Okina-gusa mistook it as Mitsukuni's own research.

sv511.text: We think even the fact-check got twisted! Outsiders muddied things, so surely Sanada's descendants kept his real name?

sv601.text: Open that later Sanada genealogy draft we mentioned, and even his own clan titled his main entry Yukimura!

sv602.text: Ironically, right under that heading it notes: first named Nobushige, called Kohaku on Mount Koya.

sv603.text: The real test came near late 1809, nearly two centuries after the Siege of Osaka.

sv604.text: A senior shogunate inspector questioned old clan genealogies, asking directly: Was Nobushige his original name?

sv605.text: Put yourself in that retainer's shoes—questioned by the shogunate about an ancestor who fought the Tokugawa!

sv606.text: A draft memo confirmed Nobushige came first; since earlier filings listed both names, what if pressed further?

sv607.text: Their planned answer: Yukimura was used exclusively after leaving the clan to join Osaka; the family used Nobushige.

sv608.text: Pinning the change on Osaka sounds convenient for everyone—but does that story hold water?

sv609.text: Remember the three letters we saw him send from inside Osaka Castle?

sv610.text: Called his Osaka name, yet all three castle letters sign Nobushige or his title—never Yukimura.

sv611.text: More awkwardly, earlier in that very memo, the retainers admit no book anywhere records him changing to Yukimura.

sv612.text: And this was just an internal memo, with no final reply in that collection. Do any Yukimura-signed papers exist?

sv613.text: Only two copies without originals survive, and modern scholars judge both to be later forgeries.

sv614.text: With zero originals, that collection's note says even the shogunate's peerage wrote Yukimura, originally Nobushige.

sv615.text: How did a name even his own clan couldn't substantiate become a household hero across all Japan?

sv701.text: The answer sat on bookstalls. In 1911, Tachikawa Bunko published volume five: The Resourceful Sanada Yukimura.

sv702.text: Priced at just twenty-five sen, its back-page ad listed the famous Zen master Ikkyu as volume one.

sv703.text: I think opening that pocket booklet a century ago worked just like picking him in games today: everyone meets Yukimura first.

sv704.text: Oddly enough, nobody could explain the name's origin, yet Sanada Yukimura outran scholarship to become a folk hero.

sv705.text: Six years later in 1917, even Tokyo University's Dai Nihon Shiryo contents listed Sanada Yukimura;

sv706.text: turn to his Kudoyama shochu letter, and the margin summary even reads: Yukimura asks for shochu.

sv707.text: We find it ironic: scholars saw Nobushige signed at the end, yet their own notes still called him Yukimura;

sv708.text: so when did that postwar praise, Japan's greatest warrior, merge for good with Sanada Yukimura?

sv801.text: In 1928 and 1938 books, Japan's finest was pinned straight onto Yukimura!

sv802.text: Just like that, a three-century-old battlefield rumor merged with a later name into the hero everyone knows today.

sv803.text: Remember our opening question? Did he ever use Yukimura while alive?

sv804.text: Modern historians reviewing surviving lifetime records confirm they leave zero evidence he ever used Yukimura.

sv805.text: As for who first coined Yukimura and why, sources found so far never say, and it remains unsettled today;

sv806.text: but we think later ages poured their respect into Yukimura,

sv807.text: while Nobushige on that foldout letter keeps the real man.

sv808.text: Case archived, and that's our story. Did you first meet Sanada Yukimura in a game, a drama, or a book?

sv809.text: Tell us in the comments, and if you love uncovering truth from primary records, subscribe to Curio Archive.
